notes:
Task and constraints: Find the minimum difference between any two node values in a BST.
Idea: Inorder dfs visits values in sorted order; compare n.val with prev, update best with the difference, then set prev to the current value.
Technique and why it applies: Sorted inorder traversal makes adjacent values sufficient to find the minimum absolute difference.
Invariant: prev is the previously visited BST value, so n.val-prev is nonnegative and covers each adjacent pair in sorted order.
Edge cases: A tree with two values returns their difference; duplicate values yield zero; the statement assumes a nonempty tree because an empty root leaves best at infinity.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(h) recursion space for n nodes and tree height h.
complexity_reason: The DFS visits every node once and updates best from each value after the first inorder visit.

notes:
Task and constraints: Find the minimum difference between values of two nodes in a BST.
Idea: Reset prev and best, traverse in inorder with dfs, compare each n.val to prev, then update prev and minimize best.
Technique and why it applies: BST inorder traversal sorts the values, so the smallest difference occurs between adjacent visited values.
Invariant: prev always stores the preceding inorder value, and best is the minimum adjacent gap observed so far.
Edge cases: A pair of nodes returns their gap; duplicate keys produce zero; root is assumed nonempty because an empty tree leaves best at Integer.MAX_VALUE. The fields are reset for each public call.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(h) call-stack space for n nodes and height h.
complexity_reason: Each node is visited once and performs a constant number of comparisons and field updates.

notes:
Task and constraints: Count unique pairs of values whose absolute difference equals k.
Idea: Return zero for negative k; count occurrences with Counter c, count values with frequency above one when k==0, otherwise count keys x for which x+k is also in c.
Technique and why it applies: Set membership counts value pairs once rather than enumerating index pairs, while Counter handles the duplicate-only zero-difference case.
Invariant: For positive k, each valid pair has a unique smaller value x, so testing x+k counts each value pair exactly once.
Edge cases: Negative k returns zero; k=0 counts each repeated value once; for k>0 duplicates do not multiply the pair count. The input array is not modified.
Complexity: O(n) expected time and O(u) space for u distinct values in Counter.
complexity_reason: Counter scans n numbers once and the final branch checks each distinct key a constant number of times.

notes:
Task and constraints: Count distinct value pairs with absolute difference k.
Idea: Reject negative k, build map c of value frequencies, count entries with frequency above one when k is zero, or count keys whose x+k is present.
Technique and why it applies: A frequency map handles zero-difference pairs, and key membership counts positive-difference pairs without duplicate index combinations.
Invariant: Each distinct key is considered once; when k>0, x is the unique smaller endpoint of its possible pair.
Edge cases: Negative k returns zero; k=0 counts a repeated value once; positive k counts each distinct value pair once. The expression x+k can overflow int outside usual problem bounds.
Complexity: O(n) expected time and O(u) space for u distinct values in the HashMap.
complexity_reason: The array is counted in one pass and each map key is inspected once in the selected counting branch.

notes:
Task and constraints: Implement encode and decode methods that map long URLs to short URLs and recover the original URL.
Idea: encode reuses url_to_id for known URLs or assigns next_id and fills both maps; decode extracts the final path segment and looks it up in id_to_url.
Technique and why it applies: Two inverse dictionaries maintain a bijection between original URLs and generated string keys.
Invariant: For every encoded URL, url_to_id and id_to_url point back to each other, and next_id advances only for a new URL.
Edge cases: Encoding the same URL twice returns the same short key; decoding a generated key returns the original URL; decoding an unknown key raises KeyError. Mappings exist only for the lifetime of this Codec instance.
Complexity: Expected O(1) time per encode/decode plus O(L) URL hashing and storage, where L is URL length; space grows with stored URLs.
complexity_reason: Each call performs a constant number of dictionary operations, while both maps retain one entry per distinct URL.

notes:
Task and constraints: Provide URL encode/decode methods using short identifiers that map back to long URLs.
Idea: encode checks toKey, assigns Integer.toString(next++) to unseen URLs and records both maps; decode extracts the substring after the final slash and looks up toUrl.
Technique and why it applies: Paired HashMaps preserve a reversible mapping while repeated encodes reuse an existing identifier.
Invariant: For each stored URL, toKey maps it to a key and toUrl maps that same key back to the URL.
Edge cases: Repeated encoding returns the same short URL; decoding a generated key restores the original; unknown keys return null from the map. The int identifier can overflow after an extreme number of unique URLs.
Complexity: Expected O(1) map operations per call plus string processing proportional to URL length; storage is O(total stored URL characters).
complexity_reason: Each call uses a constant number of map operations and stores one forward and reverse entry for each unique URL.

notes:
Task and constraints: Multiply two complex numbers encoded as strings a+bi and return the product in the same format.
Idea: parse removes the trailing i and splits at '+', converts real and imaginary parts to integers, then combine a,b,c,d using real ac-bd and imaginary ad+bc.
Technique and why it applies: Parsing separates the two integer components, and the complex multiplication identity combines them without floating-point arithmetic.
Invariant: The parsed pairs (a,b) and (c,d) represent the input numbers, and the returned real and imaginary components follow the algebraic product formula.
Edge cases: Negative real or imaginary parts are handled by int conversion; multiplying 1+1i by 1+1i returns 0+2i; input strings are assumed to follow the stated a+bi format.
Complexity: O(n+m) time and O(n+m) space for parsing and creating the result, where n and m are input-string lengths.
complexity_reason: The parser splits and converts each input string once, then formats the two computed integer components.

notes:
Task and constraints: Multiply two complex numbers supplied in a+bi string form.
Idea: parse strips the final i, splits at '+', and returns integer components in arrays a and b; the method computes ac-bd and ad+bc for the output string.
Technique and why it applies: The complex product formula combines parsed integer components directly, avoiding floating-point representation.
Invariant: a[0] and a[1] store the first input's real and imaginary parts, and b[0] and b[1] store the second's components.
Edge cases: Negative components are parsed as signed integers; (1+i)^2 returns 0+2i; the code assumes exactly one plus separator and an ending i. Java int multiplication can overflow for unrestricted component sizes.
Complexity: O(n+m) time and O(n+m) space for splitting, parsing, and output construction.
complexity_reason: Each parse call scans its input and builds a two-element array, after which fixed arithmetic creates the result.

notes:
Task and constraints: Transform each BST node to its original value plus all original values greater than it.
Idea: Traverse right subtree first, add n.val to total, replace n.val with total, then visit the left subtree.
Technique and why it applies: Reverse inorder visits BST values from largest to smallest, so a running sum accumulates all greater values before each node is updated.
Invariant: When a node is updated, total is the sum of original values already visited, including the current node's original value.
Edge cases: A null root returns null; the largest node remains unchanged; a smaller node receives the accumulated larger values. The tree is modified in place.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(h) recursion space for n nodes and height h.
complexity_reason: The DFS visits each node once and updates one running total before moving to the next node.

notes:
Task and constraints: Convert a BST to a greater tree by adding every original value greater than or equal to each node's value.
Idea: Reset sum, call dfs, visit right first, add n.val to sum, assign n.val=sum, and then traverse left.
Technique and why it applies: Reverse inorder provides descending node values, allowing one running sum to accumulate all greater-or-equal original values.
Invariant: Before updating a node, sum contains the original values of all previously visited larger nodes; after addition it includes this node's original value.
Edge cases: Null root returns null; the maximum node keeps its value; smaller nodes include accumulated larger values. The implementation mutates nodes and uses int sum, which may overflow if totals exceed int range.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(h) recursion space for n nodes and tree height h.
complexity_reason: The recursive traversal handles every node once and keeps only the running sum plus call-stack frames.

notes:
Task and constraints: Find the minimum circular difference in minutes between any two clock times.
Idea: Return zero if more than 1440 time points; convert each HH:MM string to minutes, sort vals, initialize ans with the midnight wrap gap, and minimize adjacent differences.
Technique and why it applies: Sorting places times in order, and checking adjacent gaps plus the day-boundary gap finds the closest circular pair.
Invariant: After sorting, the minimum pair is either adjacent in vals or the pair formed by the final and first times across midnight.
Edge cases: Duplicate times produce zero; 23:59 and 00:00 differ by one minute; more than 1440 entries guarantee a duplicate minute. The method assumes a nonempty list of valid times.
Complexity: O(n log n) time and O(n) space for converted and sorted minute values.
complexity_reason: The code converts n time strings, sorts n integers, and scans adjacent pairs once.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return the minimum circular minute gap among the given HH:MM strings.
Idea: Return zero for more than 1440 entries; convert each time to minutes in array a, sort it, compare adjacent gaps, and include the wrap gap from last to first.
Technique and why it applies: Sorting converts the circular clock problem into adjacent differences on a line plus one midnight boundary check.
Invariant: After sorting, any minimum gap among the times appears between adjacent entries or between the final and initial entries across midnight.
Edge cases: Duplicate times yield zero; 23:59 and 00:00 have gap one; more than 1440 values guarantee a repeated minute. The code assumes nonempty input, since a[0] and a[last] are accessed.
Complexity: O(n log n) time and O(n) space for the minute array.
complexity_reason: The method converts n strings, sorts the resulting array, and checks each adjacent pair once.

notes:
Task and constraints: Find the unique value in a sorted array where all other values occur twice, in O(log n) time and O(1) space.
Idea: Binary-search lo..hi; align mid to an even index by decrementing odd mid, compare nums[mid] with nums[mid+1], and keep the half containing the singleton.
Technique and why it applies: Pair alignment in the sorted array reveals which side has broken duplicate pairing, allowing logarithmic search.
Invariant: Before each iteration, the singleton remains within lo..hi, and the even mid is paired with its following index when duplicates lie on the left side.
Edge cases: A singleton array returns its only value; a unique value at either edge is retained by the bounds; input length is odd and nonempty by problem constraints.
Complexity: O(log n) time and O(1) extra space because each iteration halves the search interval.
complexity_reason: The loop reduces lo..hi by roughly half each time and stores only two bounds and mid.

notes:
Task and constraints: Find the single element in a sorted int array where every other value appears twice.
Idea: Use lo and hi bounds, align mid to even with mid-- when odd, compare nums[mid] and nums[mid+1], then move lo past a complete pair or set hi to mid.
Technique and why it applies: Pair-index parity shows which half contains the singleton without scanning the array.
Invariant: The singleton remains inside lo..hi, and an even mid indexes the first position of a normal adjacent pair.
Edge cases: A one-element array returns that element; a singleton at the start or end is preserved by the bounds; the array is assumed nonempty and odd-sized.
Complexity: O(log n) time and O(1) auxiliary space, since each comparison discards about half the remaining range.
complexity_reason: Each iteration halves the candidate interval and uses a fixed number of integer indices.

notes:
Task and constraints: For each 2k-character block, reverse its first k characters and leave the next k unchanged; reverse a shorter final prefix if needed.
Idea: Convert s to list a, step i by 2*k, replace a[i:i+k] with its reversed slice, and join a.
Technique and why it applies: Blockwise slicing reverses only the required prefix of each 2k segment without disturbing the remaining characters.
Invariant: At each i, all earlier blocks have been processed and characters from i+k onward within the current block remain in their original order.
Edge cases: If fewer than k characters remain, all remaining characters are reversed; if k characters remain, that prefix is reversed; k must be positive. The input string itself is immutable, so a list is used for updates.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(n) space for the character list and output string.
complexity_reason: The loop advances in 2k steps and each character is copied or reversed a constant number of times.

notes:
Task and constraints: Reverse the first k characters of each 2k block while preserving the following k characters.
Idea: Convert s to char array a; for each i incremented by 2*k, set l=i and r=min(i+k-1,last), then swap inward until l>=r.
Technique and why it applies: In-place reversal of each block prefix matches the required pattern without changing the next k characters.
Invariant: Each iteration changes only indices from i through min(i+k-1,last), leaving the rest of that 2k block untouched.
Edge cases: A final block shorter than k is fully reversed; a single character stays unchanged; k must be positive. Java char[] makes swaps mutable and the method returns a new String.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(n) space for the char array and returned string.
complexity_reason: The outer loop advances by 2k and each character participates in at most one reversal.

notes:
Task and constraints: For each binary matrix cell, return its distance to the nearest zero.
Idea: Initialize dist to -1, enqueue every zero with distance zero, then BFS to unvisited orthogonal neighbors and assign each distance as the current distance plus one.
Technique and why it applies: Multi-source BFS expands simultaneously from all zero cells, reaching each cell along a shortest grid path.
Invariant: When a cell is first assigned and enqueued, BFS guarantees its distance is minimal because queue levels increase in order.
Edge cases: A zero has distance zero; a cell adjacent to a zero gets distance one; the matrix is assumed nonempty and contains at least one zero under usual constraints. Unreachable cells would remain -1.
Complexity: O(mn) time and O(mn) space for dist and the queue, since each cell is enqueued at most once.
complexity_reason: All zero cells seed the queue, and each matrix cell is assigned and removed from the queue at most once.

notes:
Task and constraints: Compute every cell's Manhattan distance to its nearest zero in a binary matrix.
Idea: Fill d with -1, enqueue all zero positions, then use dirs to visit orthogonal neighbors; assign each unvisited neighbor the current distance plus one and enqueue it.
Technique and why it applies: Multi-source BFS computes shortest distances from the entire set of zero cells in one traversal.
Invariant: A cell receives its shortest distance when first discovered because BFS processes positions in nondecreasing distance order.
Edge cases: Zero cells stay at zero; cells next to a zero receive one; the implementation assumes nonempty rectangular input and at least one zero for all distances to be resolved.
Complexity: O(mn) time and O(mn) space for the distance matrix and queue, as each cell is enqueued at most once.
complexity_reason: The code scans all cells to seed zero positions and then visits each cell and its four neighbors at most once.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return the longest path length between any two tree nodes, measured in edges.
Idea: height returns zero for null, recursively gets l and r, updates best with l+r, and returns one plus the larger height.
Technique and why it applies: Postorder height computation considers the longest path passing through each node while calculating the heights needed by its parent.
Invariant: At each node, l and r are the child heights, so l+r is the diameter of a path whose highest point is that node.
Edge cases: An empty tree returns zero; a single node has diameter zero edges; a root with two leaf children has diameter two. The tree is assumed acyclic.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(h) recursion space for n nodes and tree height h.
complexity_reason: The height recursion visits every node once and computes the diameter candidate from its two child heights.

notes:
Task and constraints: Compute the binary tree's diameter in edges, the longest path between any two nodes.
Idea: Reset best, call height(root), compute left and right heights recursively, update best with l+r, and return 1+max(l,r).
Technique and why it applies: Postorder recursion combines subtree heights and checks the path passing through each node.
Invariant: For every node, l and r give the longest downward edge counts in its children, so l+r is the longest path through that node.
Edge cases: An empty tree returns zero; a single node has diameter zero; two leaf children give diameter two. best is reset for each call, and recursion depth can reach the height of a skewed tree.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(h) call-stack space for n nodes and height h.
complexity_reason: Each node's height is calculated once and its l+r candidate is compared with best.
